title: LinkedIn Growth Hacks You Need in 2025 | Tom Hunt
speakers_and_attribution: Adam Robinson participates alongside guest Tom Hunt, introduced as Fame's founder and CEO, and a facilitating co-host whose name is not securely established by the captions. Adam references Pete during the discussion, but that does not conclusively identify every co-host turn. A pitch-segment guest is introduced as Gajan Retnosaba of Spiralize; the name is an unverified automatic transcription. Tom owns the seven-part LinkedIn framework, Fame recruitment results and his marketing backstory. Adam owns the explicitly contextualized RB2B, prior newsletter-app, layoff, pricing and competitor-dispute accounts. The opening montage contains repeated excerpts with mixed attribution. The closing cold-email excerpt has an unidentified speaker and ends mid-sentence.
summary: Tom Hunt explains his observational approach to LinkedIn growth: human photographs, simple curiosity hooks, widely relatable topics, short stories, easy reading, engaging endings and controversy that invites substantive comments. Live post reviews translate these ideas into specific editing choices. He acknowledges that viral HR content does not align neatly with Fame's marketing buyers, although it improved recruitment. Adam contributes his approach to scannable copy, company storytelling and building in public, including disclosing layoffs against executive advice and soliciting feedback after already developing a solution. The final third examines omitted nuance, reputational costs and the emotional impact of criticism. Adam explicitly concedes that his claim that an established competitor feared his three-week-old startup was not realistic. Despite the opening promise, the episode provides no attributable revenue or customer-acquisition result from Tom's largest viral post.

key_learnings.claim: The pitch guest presents aggregated A/B-test outcomes as a way to prioritize experiments, demonstrating a lead form over a product-interface background for RB2B. The proposed mechanism is making the product feel immediately accessible after completing the form.
key_learnings.speaker: Gajan Retnosaba, captioned name; Spiralize guest
key_learnings.caveat: A vendor pitch and proposed RB2B experiment, not an implemented RB2B improvement. Dataset quality and causal transfer between companies are not verified.

key_learnings.claim: Tom recommends testing a single photograph with a clearly visible human face to interrupt scrolling. He treats his own photographs as recognition-building assets, while acknowledging that matching every image to every daily post is impractical.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: His experience, not a platform-wide causal finding. His practical qualification about relevance appears at 00:21:25–00:22:02.

key_learnings.claim: Tom's LinkedIn recommendations come from almost daily posting and close attention to performance, rather than controlled split tests. He notes that comparing posts months apart is confounded by possible algorithm changes.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: Explicit methodological limitation: repeated observation does not isolate image, topic or timing effects.

key_learnings.claim: Tom favors a simple, curiosity-producing statement in the opening line. He says number-based hooks have worked less well for him than for the hosts, and develops the post concept before writing the hook.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: Personal results rather than a universal rejection of numbers. Tom says he has not used AI to write the posts under discussion.

key_learnings.claim: Topic breadth constrains potential engagement: Tom finds workplace and HR stories more widely relatable on LinkedIn than marketing or bootstrapping content. He openly identifies a mismatch between his strongest attention topics and the marketing buyers who purchase Fame's services.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: These are Tom's content categories, not approved pillars for Adam. Reach is not shown to equal qualified demand.

key_learnings.claim: Founder content can produce business value through recruitment even when it attracts the wrong buying audience. Tom credits workplace content with more account-manager applicants, better hiring options and lower acquisition cost for talent.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: Fame self-report. Tom describes this benefit as particularly relevant to service businesses; no recruiting-cost amount or causal attribution analysis is supplied.

key_learnings.claim: Tom uses relatively short stories because he believes readers process them more readily than abstract exposition, especially when the situations are familiar workplace experiences.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: His explanation of observed performance; the psychological mechanism is speculative.

key_learnings.claim: Tom runs posts through Hemingway to remove complexity and aims for extremely easy reading. He believes unfamiliar words interrupt reading and reduce the behaviors that help a post spread.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: A guest's editing practice and algorithm hypothesis, not verified LinkedIn ranking guidance or Adam's established writing standard.

key_learnings.claim: Adam wants internet copy to convey its essential meaning through a quick scan. He considers large paragraphs intimidating after the reader expands a LinkedIn post and believes they cause abandonment.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Qualitative copywriting judgment; no measured abandonment or engagement effect is provided.

key_learnings.claim: The co-host recommends revealing the subject and reader payoff early, so readers understand why to continue. The discussion frames a useful hook as a balance between curiosity and visible relevance.
key_learnings.speaker: Facilitating co-host, with a brief panel interjection
key_learnings.caveat: The co-host explicitly addresses Adam and Tom, so this passage should not be treated as Adam's own statement. Attribution of the short interjection is less certain.

key_learnings.claim: Tom has moved away from routinely ending posts with a generic agreement question. He still wants endings that prompt action, but now accepts an emotional or memorable ending as an alternative to an explicit call to comment.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: A change in Tom's practice. He calls the old tactic cheap; he does not provide comparative results proving the newer approach performs better.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says he tries to end posts with a satisfying emotional payoff. He also believes alliteration, progressively shorter lines and the visual shape of the ending help readers reach and appreciate the final point.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: The captioned adjective 'koi' is unclear. The claims about increased engagement and reading time are Adam's qualitative interpretation.

key_learnings.claim: In a live review, Tom recommends putting one idea in the opening line, removing duplicated setup, using one image and moving a distracting photo explanation into a comment. He preserves the author's stylistic choices when they are intentional.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: Recommendations for one submitted post. His prediction of doubled engagement is not a reported outcome.

key_learnings.claim: Adam reacts negatively to an overtly promotional company post and says he uses LinkedIn to connect with people and be moved by stories. He recommends recasting that material through a personal profile, while allowing that the original creative might have a retargeting use.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: His personal reaction and recommendation, not evidence that all company-page or paid content fails.

key_learnings.claim: The co-host says the team selected posts for paid amplification based on prior organic performance, with the best candidates generally being content that did not look like product advertising.
key_learnings.speaker: Facilitating co-host
key_learnings.caveat: Team practice as described by the co-host; no campaign spend, conversion results or precise company scope is supplied.

key_learnings.claim: Tom advises asking only one question at the end of a post. Adam agrees and connects this to the single-call-to-action guidance he and Pete gave customers of his earlier email newsletter application.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson, responding to Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: Adam's accompanying fivefold conversion assertion lacks a dataset, period and baseline; it is separately recorded in the metric ledger.

key_learnings.claim: Tom identifies the reviewed business pitch as bottom-of-funnel content and therefore would not expect mass engagement, even after improving its execution.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: A useful distinction between funnel purpose and reach; the episode does not report whether this post converted.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says he rarely presents RB2B through a direct product pitch. Instead, he treats the company as a character in an unfolding story, discussing its successes, problems and behavior.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: His stated content practice at the time of recording, not a complete audit of his posts or a rule against explaining the product elsewhere.

key_learnings.claim: Adam views avoiding a direct company pitch as part of earning attention on LinkedIn, with interested readers discovering the business afterward. He recommends a profile link label that clearly describes the next action.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: He favors a website-visit label over an ambiguous services label in the specific reviewed profile; no click-through comparison is supplied.

key_learnings.claim: Tom's review of an SEO-related post again prioritizes a single clear hook, removing redundant explanation, using a human image tied to the story and bringing the ending back to that person. He retains decorative style only when it matches the author's normal expression.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: Specific editorial suggestions, not evidence that screenshots never work. The following discussion supplies an exception.

key_learnings.claim: Adam acknowledges a period when simple screenshots of notable people's tweets worked well, and confirms using that approach when Tommy Clark advised him. His current hook-checking exercise is to look for only one or two seconds, look away and assess whether the line immediately creates interest.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Historical tactic with no dates or performance figures. His explanation for why tweet screenshots spread is speculative.

key_learnings.claim: The co-host describes paradox as a recurring source of strong hooks in Adam's Monday sessions with Alec: a surprising contradiction can make the room immediately recognize a promising opening.
key_learnings.speaker: Facilitating co-host
key_learnings.caveat: Observation about Adam's process from another participant, not Adam's direct self-report. The example under discussion is recognized as a joke post.

key_learnings.claim: Tom believes long comments from people outside one's immediate network are especially powerful distribution signals. His seventh tactic is provoking those comments by agitating a shared issue or leaving out nuance that specialists will want to add.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: Unverified algorithm theory with acknowledged reputational risk. Tom admits deliberately removing detail in some posts; this tactic must not be assigned to Adam as a general belief.

key_learnings.claim: Tom illustrates omitted nuance with a remote-work post that attracted tax and compliance objections and a canceled one-on-one post that omitted his prior communication with the employee. He says he deleted a different firing-related post after readers interpreted it as boasting about dismissal.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: Tom's accounts of posts and reactions. The transcript does not establish the legal merits of the compliance objections, and he cannot recall the deleted post's exact hook.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says he disclosed a layoff despite his executive team's objections because omitting it could undermine the credibility and informational value of his building-in-public content. He retained the post despite intense criticism.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: The affected company is not identified. This is a specific decision demonstrating a preference for disclosure, not an approved overarching mission or an independently validated account.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says public discussion of RB2B's early pricing problems yielded substantial product insight even though the team had already developed its likely solution. He later repeated the format, sometimes presenting himself as less decided than he actually was to invite advice.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: He explicitly says the first discussion did not materially change the planned decision. The exact original pricing is unclear in the captions.

key_learnings.claim: Tom links his aggressive pursuit of LinkedIn attention to an earlier online-marketing background that trained him to exploit temporary opportunities. He acknowledges that criticism hurts and raises the unresolved tradeoff between immediate attention and long-term value.
key_learnings.speaker: Tom Hunt
key_learnings.caveat: Tom's motivation and backstory, not Adam's. No measurement of long-term reputation or commercial loss is supplied.

key_learnings.claim: Adam admits that negative comments affect him emotionally and can spoil hours of his day. He also characterizes his earlier attack on an established competitor as somewhat disingenuous, explicitly rejecting the realism of his claim that it feared his very young startup.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: The competitor is captioned as 'six sense' and later 'six cents,' apparently referring to 6sense. The underlying dispute is not independently examined here.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says RB2B built a HubSpot integration in response to customer requests and that its permission screen described its behavior with an accept-or-cancel choice. He presents subsequent accusations as an example of criticism escalating across multiple posts.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Adam's defense only. The integration, permission scope and critics' claims are not independently verified; accusations recounted here are not established facts.

key_learnings.claim: The final cold-email excerpt prioritizes reaching the inbox and the recipient's recognition of the sender over subject-line optimization.
key_learnings.speaker: Unidentified closing-excerpt speaker
key_learnings.caveat: Apparently an outro or teaser, with no secure attribution to Adam or Tom. It ends mid-sentence before completing its ranking of factors.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam says his first company was an email newsletter application and recalls advising its users alongside Pete.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: The company name, dates and Pete's formal role are not stated here.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam describes feeling current competitive pressure from frequent entrants copying and undercutting his offering.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: A personal description of market pressure at recording, not an independently established rate of competitor entry or copying.

backstory_and_values.claim: The co-host recalls that Adam's RB2B launch content centered on growth goals and avoiding mistakes from prior businesses, allowing readers to discover the product through the founder's story.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Facilitating co-host
backstory_and_values.caveat: Second-person recollection, not Adam's own account. No specific growth target or prior-business mistake is named.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam confirms that Tommy Clark previously advised his LinkedIn work and that tweet-image posts were part of that earlier approach.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: No dates, contract details or evidence of the tactic's commercial effect are given.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam's decision to disclose a layoff over executive objections shows that, in this instance, he prioritized consistency and credibility in public company reporting despite foreseeable backlash.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: Interpretation grounded in his stated rationale for one decision; it should not be promoted into an approved mission claim.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam openly acknowledges staging some requests for product advice as if he had no solution, although the team already had a direction. He also acknowledges that one competitor narrative overstated the actual situation.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: Two specific admissions within this interval. They complicate any interpretation that all his public content presents the complete contemporaneous decision state.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam describes himself as generally positive but says hostile online interactions still affect his mood, despite his inclination to say he does not care what others think.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: Self-description and situational emotional experience, not a psychological diagnosis or an approved voice attribute.

backstory_and_values.claim: Tom says he likes Fame and expects to keep running it for a long time. He would consider HR if he pursued another business because he is interested in it and already attracts attention there.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Tom Hunt
backstory_and_values.caveat: A guest's hypothetical future direction, not a launched venture or Adam's business plan.

backstory_and_values.claim: Tom says his partner previously worked as a photographer and helps create his image backlog. Coffee is something he likes and incorporates into his personal presentation, rather than a fully preplanned engagement mechanism.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Tom Hunt
backstory_and_values.caveat: Tom's personal context only. His explanation of coffee imagery's effectiveness is explicitly retrospective speculation.

backstory_and_values.claim: Tom describes a pre-entrepreneurship background in intensive online marketing and says he first connected with Adam through his own podcast, where Adam appeared as a guest.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Tom Hunt
backstory_and_values.caveat: The podcast connection is stated separately at 00:51:34–00:51:42. Neither account supplies dates; neither is Adam's entrepreneurial backstory.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Tom Hunt's LinkedIn reach is introduced with figures of more than 300,000 likes and 175 million views; the host also promises attendees the ability to create a post with 375,000 likes.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Facilitating co-host
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Promotional framing, not independently verified reporting. The view-count period and whether it is cumulative are unstated. The 375,000 figure is an exaggerated instructional promise, not a participant achievement.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Tom presents six tactics as sufficient to reach roughly 1,000 likes and a seventh as potentially producing 10,000–100,000 likes; his initial statement suggests the first milestone could happen within a week.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Tom Hunt
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Forecast or promotional claim, not a measured success rate. The scale is repeated around 00:09:07–00:09:13, with compressed automatic-caption wording.

metrics_and_dates.claim: The live show's pitch segment begins with a reported 294 live guests. The co-host recalls a demo-request record around 26 or the high twenties, and more than a dozen in each of the preceding couple of weeks.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Facilitating co-host
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Approximate show-level self-report at recording. Audience demo requests are not verified completed bookings, qualified pipeline or sales.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Spiralize initially offers a 30% lift within the first 90 days with no fee unless it hits the number. When asked whether this means revenue, the guest says the goal depends on the client and is often a sales-qualified lead measure.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Gajan Retnosaba, captioned name; Spiralize guest
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Commercial guarantee rather than achieved client performance. The exact lead acronym is unclear in the captions; it must not be recorded as a guaranteed 30% revenue increase.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Spiralize claims to scrape 34,000 actively testing sites and shows a form-over-interface pattern reportedly tested by 158 companies, assigning it approximately a 53% chance of winning.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Gajan Retnosaba, captioned name; Spiralize guest
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Vendor self-report with no collection period or validation method. The speaker later calls 158 the number of times the test has run; companies and test runs should not be silently equated.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Spiralize proposes running 10 tests over 90 days, expecting about three wins and approximately 30% lift. The guest then says payment applies at 30% and there is no fee below 10%.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Gajan Retnosaba, captioned name; Spiralize guest
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Projected program results, not an RB2B achievement. Treatment of a 10%–29% lift is unstated and the fee wording differs from the initial guarantee.

metrics_and_dates.claim: The co-host counts approximately 10 audience demo requests during Spiralize's pitch response and says more are still arriving.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Facilitating co-host
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Live count of expressed interest for Spiralize, not a final booking tally or revenue for Adam's companies.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Tom says he has posted almost daily for approximately three years and closely reviewed performance. He describes trying to publish seven days a week.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Tom Hunt
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Guest self-report relative to recording; no precise start date. The seven-day ambition appears at 00:21:39–00:21:47 and is not proof of uninterrupted daily publishing.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Tom estimates that his marketing and business/bootstrapping posts receive roughly 10% of the engagement of his HR and workplace posts.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Tom Hunt
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Approximate personal comparison, with no date range, sample size or engagement denominator.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Fame's account-manager applications reportedly increased from roughly 50 per month to 500 per month when Tom's workplace content began gaining traction.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Tom Hunt
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Guest company self-report. Exact before-and-after months are unstated; applicants are not hires or FTE, and no financial recruiting-cost reduction is quantified.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Tom's personal content specifications include a face occupying approximately 5%–10% of an image and a Hemingway readability target of grade one, sometimes accepting grade two but rejecting grade three.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Tom Hunt
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Prescriptive heuristics, not business results. The readability thresholds are stated at 00:17:25–00:17:45.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Adam recalls telling newsletter-app customers that a single CTA could produce five times the conversion rate of using multiple actions.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical recollection of advice, not a substantiated company performance metric. No dates, baseline, study or definition of conversion is supplied.

metrics_and_dates.claim: One of Tom's largest posts concerns a team member working from another country for six weeks. Later discussion refers to the large post using both 375,000 and 309,000 likes, while Tom recalls approximately 50 compliance-related comment threads.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Tom Hunt and a host asking about the post
metrics_and_dates.caveat: The six-week scenario and approximate thread count are Tom's account; the varying like counts occur in a host question at 00:43:35–00:43:44. No measurement date or reconciled total is available.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Adam dates the layoff he publicly discussed to 'last year' and estimates the reactions as roughly 75% sympathetic and 25% hostile. He says the post performed very well but was not his best ever.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Relative to an unspecified recording date; 2024 is only implied if recording occurred in 2025. Company, employee count and engagement totals are absent. The percentages are informal estimates.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Adam places RB2B's initial pricing problem in its first six weeks. The intended free-and-paid structure is captioned unclearly as 'free and five in 4.95,' and he characterizes conversion as absent or inadequate.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Do not normalize the price into $495 or another amount. 'Nobody's converting' is a paraphrased post premise, not a verified 0% conversion measurement; no launch date is supplied.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Adam says his startup was three weeks old when he portrayed an established competitor as afraid of it.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical relative age with no calendar date. He explicitly corrects the fear claim as unrealistic.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Near the close, a host estimates that the weekly B2B live show attracted unique attendance in the mid-400s.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Host; exact identity uncertain
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Approximate unique-attendee count, not concurrent attendance. It is therefore not directly comparable with the 294 live guests reported early in the episode.

tensions_and_corrections: The episode promises to examine whether Tom's viral post drove business, but the only concrete commercial-adjacent outcome quantified is Fame's recruitment application growth. No attributable revenue, ARR, profit, customer count or sales pipeline result is given for the viral post.

Tom's largest-post like counts vary across the introduction and later discussion: 300,000-plus, 375,000 and 309,000. The 175 million views figure has no defined period or scope. Preserve these as unreconciled statements.
Tom's confident performance promises exceed his stated evidence method: he explicitly says he has never run controlled split tests and acknowledges algorithm changes as a confounder.
HR and workplace content attracts Tom's largest audience, while Fame sells to marketers. Recruitment provides a partial business rationale, but does not resolve the buyer-alignment problem.

Tom once routinely used generic agreement questions and now largely avoids them as cheap engagement devices. Adam favors emotionally satisfying endings; neither position establishes one universal CTA rule.

Human images are presented as the strongest default, but Tom allows imperfect relevance for production practicality, recommends a spouse's photo in one review, and Adam recalls successful tweet screenshots. These qualifications prevent a literal rule that every post must show its author.
The co-host and Tom recommend removing hashtags, including a secondhand claim attributed to Alec Paul. These are source-date-specific platform beliefs, not independently verified enduring rules.

Tom's omitted-nuance tactic may stimulate expertise-sharing and distribution while creating misleading impressions. His deletion of a firing post shows a reputational boundary rather than unlimited tolerance for backlash.

Adam argues that omitting a layoff would compromise his content's credibility, yet admits portraying product decisions as more unresolved than they were and overstating a competitor's fear. These are substantive tensions in his presentation of building in public.
Adam corrects his own stance on criticism: although he likes to say it does not bother him, he says it can spoil an hour, several hours or an afternoon.

Spiralize's initial no-fee-unless-30%-lift promise changes to no fee below 10%, leaving intermediate outcomes unclear. Its 53% estimate for one pattern and roughly three wins across 10 proposed tests concern different scopes and should not be silently reconciled.

Spiralize's lift is not established as revenue lift. Its named customer logos, scraped-site scope and claimed test results remain guest sales assertions; several company and personal names may be miscaptioned.

The closing preview mentions a future guest captioned as Ryan Alice and a company captioned as Eye Contact, with a vague claim of making millions. This is an unverified promotional comparison about another person, not Adam's backstory or a usable quantified proof point.

Publication on 2025-04-23 does not establish the recording date, launch date, layoff date or dates of historical posts. The announcement that the recording would ideally appear by Friday reinforces the distinction.
The final cold-email clip ends abruptly and cannot be securely attributed. Its incomplete claims should not become Adam's established strategy.
